blocks.title: Honors — justify the decomposition
blocks.markdown: CPA breaks a vector into components using sine and cosine. Honors does the same — then defends **why** that trig is the right trig, instead of guessing which function goes where.

## Why sine, why cosine?

For a vector of magnitude $R$ at angle $\theta$ measured from the **+x axis**:

- $R_x = R\cos\theta$ — the **adjacent** side of the right triangle the vector forms.
- $R_y = R\sin\theta$ — the **opposite** side.

The choice isn't a rule to memorize; it follows from *where you measured the angle from*. Measure $\theta$ from the y-axis instead and sine and cosine swap. So before decomposing, the honors question is always: **what is my angle measured from, and which leg of the triangle is that?**

The components must also rebuild the original: $R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2}$. If they don't, the decomposition is wrong — a built-in check.

blocks.frame: I used $R_x = R\cos\theta$ and $R_y = R\sin\theta$ because my angle $\theta$ was measured from ___, which makes the x-component the ___ side of the triangle. If the angle were measured from ___ instead, I would ___.
blocks.prompt: JUSTIFY: For 2026-XJ's velocity at an angle, you split it into components. Explain WHY you assigned cosine to one axis and sine to the other — tie it to where the angle is measured from and which side of the right triangle each component is.

blocks.title: State the assumption
blocks.markdown: Decomposing into perpendicular x and y components assumes those two axes are **independent** — motion along x doesn't affect motion along y. That independence is what lets us treat a 2-D problem as two separate 1-D problems. It's a powerful assumption; name it, because later (projectiles, forces on the asteroid) it's exactly the assumption that does the heavy lifting.
